tutor_message.content:
You're definitely focusing on the key concepts here! You've identified the need to consider both special cases (such as zero and negatives) and the fundamental property that defines powers of three: repeated divisibility by 3 should ultimately reduce n to 1, if n is truly a power of three.

Remember, the underlying principle for recognizing powers of a number is that, given a base (here, 3), powers are constructed by multiplying the base by itself repeatedly, starting from 1 (since 3⁰ = 1). This is why, after dividing by 3 as many times as possible, only powers of three will become exactly 1; any other starting value will either not be divisible by 3 at all or will stop at some other number.

This principle is frequently used not only for "power of three" problems, but also for powers of other numbers (like two, five, etc.), making the concept quite valuable for a range of coding interviews and algorithmic problems.
